$comment: Behavioural cases for the mn fork's enforcement layer, drawn from failures
that actually happened in this author's projects rather than invented for
the test. Each case is stated the way the evals guidance asks: a situation
two people would independently agree on, with one expected verdict.
Why these exist alongside the per-hook unit tests: a unit test asks 'does
this function return deny'. These ask 'given the situation that burned us,
does the harness as a whole refuse'. The distinction matters because every
one of these passed its unit tests at the time the failure happened — the
gap was in which situations were wired, not in whether the code worked.
`source` names where the failure is recorded. `verdict` is what the harness
must do: block (refuse and say why), allow (proceed silently), or warn
(proceed but say something). A case whose verdict is `allow` is doing real
work: it pins a legitimate shape the guard must NOT block, which is the
failure mode that makes people disable a guard entirely.

cases.source: mn-fork-worklog: 26 of 174 phases carry same-wave plans touching overlapping files
cases.situation: A plan declares libs/rpg/ports/book.port.ts; the executor writes libs/rpg/domain/entity.ts, which no plan in the phase names.
cases.because: blast-radius would report this at verify:pre, after the commit. The same question at the write costs one redirect.

cases.source: measured: ~10% of real files_modified entries are globs or directories
cases.situation: A plan declares libs/rpg/domain/** and the executor writes a file three levels inside it.
cases.because: Treating a declared glob as a literal filename would deny the writes it exists to permit — the false positive that trains people to turn a guard off.

cases.source: design: SUMMARY/VERIFICATION/STATE are written by the harness and never appear in files_modified
cases.situation: The executor writes its own SUMMARY.md while a plan with a narrow scope is in flight.
cases.because: Guarding the harness's own bookkeeping would block the workflow instead of protecting it.

cases.source: measured: 14% of plans carry an empty files_modified
cases.situation: The running plan declares no files at all, and the executor writes something.
cases.because: An empty declaration is blast-radius's refusal to make at verify:pre, where it fails rather than passes. Reading it here as 'declares nothing, so permits everything' would disarm the guard exactly on the phases where the planner was sloppiest — so this hook stays out of it deliberately, and the case pins that it is a decision rather than an oversight.

cases.source: assertion-ratchet exists because this happens; SpecBench measures the general form
cases.situation: A test file with three assertions is rewritten with two, while the third's behaviour is unchanged.
cases.because: Deleting the check is the cheapest way to make a red suite green, and the one failure a green suite cannot report.

cases.source: the obvious evasion of a line-count check
cases.situation: The third assertion is commented out in place rather than deleted.
cases.because: A commented-out assertion is a deleted assertion. Counting it as live would let the deletion through disguised as a comment.

cases.situation: A fourth assertion is added to an existing test file.
cases.because: The guard defends the count from below. Blocking growth would make it an obstacle to the thing it is protecting.

cases.source: ucars SUMMARYs: "the plan's resolver snippet does not compile", "the plan's useInject would have crashed web and mobile"
cases.situation: An executor finishes while the project's own typecheck still fails.
cases.because: The work is not finished while the project's own checks are red, and lint/typecheck are the cheapest verifier in the system — deterministic, already written, and unable to be optimistic.

cases.source: design; the same rule autonomous.md applies to loop gates
cases.situation: workflow.exit_gate names a command that does not exist.
cases.because: A gate that cannot run is a configuration problem, not a code problem. Reporting it as a code failure is how a gate earns the reputation that gets it disabled.

cases.source: ucars retrospective: "worktree 380 commits behind main at start"
cases.situation: A worktree is created from a base far behind the main checkout.
cases.because: Plans written against a base that has already moved have to be redone. Refusing costs one command; proceeding costs the phase.

cases.situation: The main checkout has no .mcp.json to copy into the new worktree.
cases.because: The phase may not need the tool. Refusing to create a worktree over an optional convenience is how people come to distrust isolation and turn it off.

cases.source: ucars retrospective: NN-HUMAN-UAT.md invented by hand because items "got silently dropped"
cases.situation: The phase's UAT file lists a check the verifier deferred to a human, and nobody ran it.
cases.because: The phase's own report says nobody checked. Shipping past that makes the record a formality.

cases.source: design: the verifier owns the gaps_found / human_needed verdict
cases.situation: The UAT item was run and failed.
cases.because: A failed manual check is a known defect whose verdict belongs to verification. This gate asks only whether anything went unrun; blocking here too would make two mechanisms fight over one decision.

cases.situation: The phase produced no UAT file at all.
cases.because: Requiring the artifact would block a phase for having nothing to check — the inverse of blast-radius, where an empty declaration IS the defect.
